name: ParAMD (parallel approximate minimum degree ordering)
baseline: SuiteSparse AMD (single-threaded approximate minimum degree fill-reducing ordering)
workload: Fill-reducing AMD ordering time and fill-in on 9 SuiteSparse Matrix Collection matrices (pre2, nd24k, ldoor, dielFilterV3real, Flan_1565, HV15R, Queen_4147, stokes, nlpkkt240); median of five random row permutations, ParAMD at 1 and 64 threads versus SuiteSparse AMD.
claimed_speedup: 64 threads: 2.85x (nd24k) to 8.51x (nlpkkt240) faster than SuiteSparse AMD (pre2 3.25x, ldoor 4.64x, dielFilterV3real 5.92x, Flan_1565 6.11x, HV15R 6.21x, Queen_4147 6.18x, stokes 7.95x). Single thread: 0.44x to 1.01x, i.e. slower than SuiteSparse on 8 of 9 matrices. Fill-in ratio versus SuiteSparse at 64 threads: 0.98x to 1.16x.
compiler_and_flags: GCC v13.2.1 (must support '#pragma omp atomic compare'), OpenMP, CMake default build type Release; scripts/ in the repo (all.sh, scaling.sh) reproduce the table
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 (64 cores) for the committed exemplar outputs; README says benchmarks need at least 64 physical cores and 256 GB RAM
tradeoffs: Approximate parallel variant: ordering quality is slightly worse (fill-in up to 1.16x SuiteSparse AMD in the committed table). Needs many cores to pay off; at one thread it is slower than SuiteSparse AMD. Provides libparamd.so, a paramd.h header and a CLI; reads Matrix Market input; OpenMP; relaxation factors (mult, lim, mem) are tunable.
caveats: Authors' own benchmark (PASSIONLab, accompanying arXiv preprint 2504.17097 was not opened). The committed plots/scaling.csv is one exemplar run on one machine. The headline speedups compare 64 threads to the single-threaded SuiteSparse AMD, so they measure parallel scaling, not per-core efficiency. SuiteSparse AMD version and its build flags are not stated in the README. Repository is young (4 commits, April to November 2025) and has few users.
found_via: GitHub topic page https://github.com/topics/sparse-matrix?l=c%2B%2B&o=desc&s=stars&page=2 (WebFetch), then the PASSIONLab/ParAMD README and plots/scaling.csv

name: CVR (Compressed Vectorization-oriented sparse Row) SpMV
baseline: Intel MKL CSR SpMV (paper also compares CSR5, VHCC, CSR-I and ESB)
workload: Parallel SpMV (y = y + A*x) on 58 scale-free and HPC sparse matrices from the SuiteSparse Matrix Collection and SNAP, run on a 68-core Intel Xeon Phi 7250 (Knights Landing) with MCDRAM in flat mode.
claimed_speedup: Scale-free matrices: up to 40x (2.84x on average) over MKL and up to 1.70x (1.33x on average) over the best other approach. HPC matrices: up to 17x (1.22x on average) over MKL and up to 1.57x (1.10x on average) over the best other approach. CVR typically has the lowest preprocessing overhead.
compiler_and_flags: Intel C/C++ compiler 17.04, 'icpc -O3 -ansi -ansi-alias -xMIC-AVX512 -qopenmp' (Makefile); paper states flags '-xMIC-AVX512 -O3'
hardware: Intel Xeon Phi 7250 (Knights Landing, 68 cores, 16 GB MCDRAM, 96 GB DDR4), CentOS 7.3
tradeoffs: Format conversion from CSR is required (preprocessing time is reported in the paper and in the program output). Targets AVX-512 and the Intel compiler; needs numactl to place data in MCDRAM. Research artifact (CGO'18, artifact appendix in the paper) rather than a general library API.
caveats: Peer-reviewed CGO 2018 paper, but the MKL, ESB and CSR-I baselines are supplied only as executables (source withheld), so the MKL comparison cannot be audited from source; arguably tier A if the provided scripts are rerun. Knights Landing is discontinued hardware and the MKL version is from 2017, so the margins over MKL on current CPUs are unknown. Over the best non-MKL competitor the average gain is modest (1.10x on HPC matrices).
found_via: GitHub topic page https://github.com/topics/spmv?l=c%2B%2B&o=desc&s=stars (WebFetch), then the CVR repo page, README and the paper PDF stored in the repo

name: spla (generalized sparse linear algebra, vendor-agnostic GPU)
workload: GraphBLAS-style graph algorithms (BFS, SSSP, PageRank, triangle counting) on 13 SuiteSparse/SNAP/LAW graphs (coAuthorsCiteseer up to road_central, indochina-2004 with 302M edges), spla on a GTX 1070 GPU versus LAGraph on the CPU of the same machine; also integrated Intel and AMD GPUs.
claimed_speedup: README log-scale bar chart of speedup over LAGraph (SuiteSparse), values read off the chart so approximate: PageRank roughly 7x to 65x, SSSP roughly 1.4x to 23x, triangle counting roughly 4x to 12x, BFS roughly 0.7x to 3.6x (slower than LAGraph on some graphs). README text also claims 'much faster than scipy or networkx' and better PageRank than Gunrock and competitive results against GraphBLAST. No exact numbers are printed.
hardware: Ubuntu 20.04, Intel Core i7-6700 3.40GHz (4 cores), 64 GB DDR4, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1070 8 GB (also Intel HD Graphics 530, AMD GFX1036, Intel Arc A770, AMD Vega Frontier Edition)
tradeoffs: GPU-resident sparse linear algebra with C/C++ API and Python bindings (PyPI). Runs on Intel, Nvidia and AMD GPUs including integrated ones. Graph-analytics oriented (GraphBLAS semirings), not a solver library. Needs a GPU to see the gains.
caveats: Numbers exist only as a chart image (docs/stats/rq1_rel.png); the speedups here are read off the log axis. The comparison is a GTX 1070 GPU against LAGraph on a 4-core CPU, not a like-for-like device comparison. Compiler and flags are not stated; baseline runs were done by the library authors. README says the project is under heavy development and not ready for usage. BFS does not beat the baseline on every graph.
found_via: GitHub topic page https://github.com/topics/sparse-matrix?l=c%2B%2B&o=desc&s=stars (WebFetch), then the spla README and docs/stats/rq1_rel.png

name: SPbLA (sparse Boolean linear algebra on GPU; cuBool and clBool backends)
baseline: SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS (CPU) plus CUSP, cuSPARSE and clSPARSE (GPU)
workload: Boolean sparse matrix-matrix multiplication M x M and element-wise addition M + M^2 on 10 SuiteSparse/SNAP/LAW graph matrices (e.g. amazon-2008, web-Google, roadNet-CA, netherlands_osm); time in ms and memory in MB; GTX 1070 GPU versus i7-6700 CPU.
claimed_speedup: Paper: Boolean-specialized operations 'can be up to 5 times faster and consume up to 4 times less memory' than generic non-Boolean operations from CUSP or cuSPARSE. From Table II (M x M, derived from page data): cuBool 1.9 ms vs SuiteSparse 7.9 ms on matrix 0, 23.2 vs 257.6 ms on matrix 2, 33.3 vs 369.5 ms on matrix 3, 41.8 vs 673.3 ms on matrix 4 (about 4x to 16x); cuSPARSE took 4761.3 ms on matrix 4. Not uniformly faster: cuSPARSE is faster on matrix 1 (1.7 vs 2.4 ms) and CUSP/cuSPARSE are often as fast or faster for M + M^2 (Table III), where cuBool's advantage is lower memory.
hardware: Ubuntu 20.04, Intel Core i7-6700 3.40GHz, 64 GB DDR4, GeForce GTX 1070 8 GB
tradeoffs: Boolean (structure-only) matrices only; CUDA (cuBool) and OpenCL (clBool) backends plus a CPU fallback, Python bindings. Much lower peak GPU memory than the generic libraries in the paper's tables. The GPU baselines treat nonzero floats as true, so they do more work per element than a Boolean kernel.
caveats: Paper PDF text does not state its venue (it sits in a 2021/GRAPL folder of the YaccConstructor/articles repo), so peer review is unconfirmed and the tier stays C; B if the workshop venue is confirmed. The baseline comparison is GPU versus a CPU library and a Boolean kernel versus non-Boolean kernels, which the SpBench README itself calls 'not entirely fair'. Compiler and flags not stated. Public benchmark code exists at https://github.com/EgorOrachyov/SpBench (opened) but was not rerun.
found_via: GitHub topic pages https://github.com/topics/sparse-matrix?l=c%2B%2B&o=desc&s=stars&page=2 and https://github.com/topics/graphblas; paper PDF linked from the spbla README

name: ALBUS (SIMD and load-balanced SpMV)
baseline: CSR5 (ICS'15) and CVR (CGO'18) SpMV; the README table also lists Merge (SC'16) and Intel MKL columns but leaves them empty
workload: Parallel double-precision SpMV, GFlops, on 28 SuiteSparse/SNAP matrices (rma10, cant, mac_econ_fwd500, webbase-1M, road_usa, ...) on a dual-socket Intel Xeon Gold 6242.
claimed_speedup: README table: ALBUS has the highest GFlops on 25 of 28 matrices, e.g. rma10 94.52 vs CSR5 42.05 and CVR 65.84; mac_econ_fwd500 68.56 vs 25.33 and 40.79; dc2 65.32 vs 24.59 and 39.28; webbase-1M 34.14 vs 21.92 and 22.13. About 2.7x over CSR5 on mac_econ_fwd500 (derived from page data). CVR wins on cant (68.66 vs 65.38), ins2 (34.16 vs 23.06) and pdb1HYS (68.23 vs 65.44).
compiler_and_flags: Makefile: 'icpc -xCORE-AVX2 -qopt-prefetch=3 -fopenmp -O3' (g++ also supported); compiler version not stated
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6242, dual socket (16 cores x 2) for the table; a later README note names Dual E5-2670 v3 and Dual Xeon Silver 4110 as test platforms
tradeoffs: Research code (OpenMP and OpenMP+AVX2 variants; Albus_spmv.h and Storage_format.h) that is AVX2 and Intel compiler oriented and not packaged as a library. Published in Future Generation Computer Systems 2021 (doi 10.1016/j.future.2020.10.036, cited in the README, paper not opened).
caveats: The table has no MKL or Merge numbers and does not say how the CSR5 and CVR figures were produced or with which thread counts; the baseline sources are not in the repo. README lists inconsistent test hardware. The comparison against MKL named in the paper keywords is not shown on the page.

name: HP-SpMM-SDDMM (fast GPU SpMM for GNN graphs)
baseline: cuSPARSE 12.2 SpMM (CSR ALG2, CSR ALG3, CSR default, COO) and GE-SpMM
workload: FP32 sparse-dense matrix multiplication (SpMM) in GFLOPS, averaged over K = 32, 64 and 128 dense columns, on 17 GNN datasets (Yelp, Flickr, AIFB, BGS, AM, MUTAG, AmazonCoBuyComputer, arxiv, collab, ddi, ppa, products, protein, reddit, ...) on an NVIDIA H800.
claimed_speedup: README bar chart (GFLOPS, values read off the chart so approximate): HP-SpMM is the highest bar on all 17 datasets, e.g. about 1730 vs about 1050 for the best cuSPARSE variant on Yelp, about 1870 vs 1130 on arxiv, about 3000 vs 1920 on reddit; about equal on ddi (about 2400 vs 2370). No exact numbers are printed.
compiler_and_flags: NVCC >= 11.8 built through CMake; flags not stated in the README
hardware: NVIDIA H800 for the README figure; code requires Ampere (A100, A800) or Hopper (H100, H800) GPUs
tradeoffs: FP32 only, Ampere and Hopper GPUs only, CUDA 11.8+. Targets the sparsity patterns of GNN training graphs rather than scientific matrices. Companion code to 'Fast Sparse GPU Kernels for Accelerated Training of Graph Neural Networks' (IPDPS 2023); this repo is described as the updated version.
caveats: No LICENSE file appears in the repository root listing, so the code is treated as reference only. Results are an image; the IPDPS 2023 paper that would make this tier B covers the earlier version and was not opened. cuSPARSE is a vendor library, not one of the listed incumbents; the baseline for scientific sparse matrices could differ.
found_via: GitHub topic pages https://github.com/topics/spmm and https://github.com/topics/sparse-matrix?l=c%2B%2B&o=desc&s=stars&page=2; README image result_h800-1704017465770.png

name: Cache-Aware and GPU-Accelerated SpMV (VSJ001)
workload: CSR SpMV effective memory bandwidth (GB/s) of a hand-written one-warp-per-row CUDA kernel versus cuSPARSE on four SuiteSparse matrices (cant, consph, pdb1HYS, webbase-1M) on an A100.
claimed_speedup: 'beats NVIDIA's cuSPARSE library by 24-56 percent on regular real-world matrices': cant 1531 vs 1172 GB/s (+30.6%), consph 1557 vs 1252 GB/s (+24.4%), pdb1HYS 1718 vs 1102 GB/s (+55.8%); cuSPARSE wins on webbase-1M (847 vs 203 GB/s).
compiler_and_flags: make gpu: 'nvcc -arch=sm_80' with CUDA 12.3; CPU build 'gcc -O3 -march=native -ftree-vectorize'
hardware: NVIDIA A100 80GB (README also quotes a 1555 GB/s HBM2 peak) on the Northeastern University Explorer cluster; Intel Xeon Gold host CPUs
tradeoffs: Simple CSR-vector kernel (one warp per row, warp-shuffle reduction) with an ELL variant and a selector that skips ELL on irregular rows; CPU side adds cache tiling and AVX2 with software prefetching. Loses to cuSPARSE on irregular web-graph matrices.
caveats: Coursework-style project with four real matrices. README reports 98 to 110 percent of HBM2 peak bandwidth, which means the matrices largely fit in the A100 L2 cache, so the bandwidth numbers are cache-assisted and the win may not hold for large matrices. Only one cuSPARSE algorithm (CSR_ALG2) was compared. No LICENSE file seen. Tier A is borderline: hardware, nvcc version and architecture flag are stated and code plus CSVs are public, but only partial flags are given.

name: fast_matrix_market (parallel Matrix Market sparse matrix I/O)
baseline: C++ IOStreams (std::istream/ostream) and fscanf based Matrix Market loaders
workload: Reading and writing Matrix Market coordinate files into sparse structures with chunked parallel parsing; README plots show read and write scaling with thread count against a sequential IOStreams loader.
claimed_speedup: 'Reach >1GB/s read and write speeds on a laptop (about 25x improvement over IOStreams).'
stars_or_usage: 91 stars; bindings ship in SciPy 1.12+ as scipy.io.mmread and mmwrite
tradeoffs: C++17 library using <charconv> (fast_float and Dragonbox as fallbacks). Ready-made bindings for GraphBLAS, Eigen, CXSparse, Blaze and Armadillo, plus Python and R bindings. Supports coordinate and array formats and all field types.
caveats: This is sparse matrix file I/O, not a solver or kernel, so it is at the edge of the category. The IOStreams baseline is sequential by the author's choice (IOStreams slow down with threads because of locale locking). Laptop model, compiler and flags are not stated; the scaling plots are SVG images and run_benchmarks.sh must be run to see numbers. The README's detailed comparison data sits in the separate parse-bench repo, which was not opened.

name: TACO (Tensor Algebra Compiler)
baseline: hand-optimized sparse linear algebra and sparse tensor kernels in widely used libraries (the README does not name them; Eigen and Intel MKL are the likely comparison targets but this was not confirmed on an opened page)
workload: Generated kernels for sparse tensor algebra and sparse linear algebra expressions on CPUs and GPUs; no specific benchmark is stated on the repo page.
claimed_speedup: 'performance competitive with hand-optimized kernels in widely used libraries for both sparse tensor algebra and sparse linear algebra' (README; no numbers, and 'competitive' is not a claim of being faster)
tradeoffs: Usable as a C++ library to load tensors and compute expressions, or as a code generator that emits C functions for a given expression and format. The README links the OOPSLA 2017 paper and two technical reports (arXiv 1802.10574 on optimization, 1804.10112 on formats) for details.
caveats: Only entry in this run with no numbers; included as the single tier D because the project is notable. arxiv.org, tensor-compiler.org and the paper PDFs were blocked in this environment, so the paper speedups against named libraries could not be opened; the verifier should read the OOPSLA paper and arXiv 1802.10574 for exact baselines and ratios. The README only claims parity ('competitive'), not a win.
